Debian-based Linux distributions use two layers of package management: the low-level dpkg tool that directly manipulates .deb packages, and the high-level apt front-end that handles repository resolution, dependency management, and downloads. This reference covers both, plus nala — a modern, user-friendly wrapper around APT.
dpkg works directly with .deb package files and the installed package database. It does not handle dependencies automatically.

dpkg queries the installed package database: listing what is installed, inspecting a package's status, listing the files it provides, and finding which package owns a given file. dpkg -l # list all installed packages dpkg -l | grep nginx # find a specific package dpkg -l | head -5 # just the first few lines dpkg -s nginx # status of installed package (detailed) dpkg -p nginx # status (like -s, includes available info) dpkg -L nginx # list files installed by a package dpkg -c package.deb # list contents of a .deb file (before installing) dpkg -S /etc/nginx/nginx.conf # find which package owns a file dpkg --get-selections # list all packages with install status

dpkg installs .deb files directly and removes packages at the low level. It does not resolve dependencies — prefer apt unless you are working with a specific .deb file or repairing package state. # Install a local .deb file dpkg -i package.deb dpkg --install package.deb # Remove a package (keep config files) dpkg -r nginx dpkg --remove nginx # Purge a package (remove everything including configs) dpkg -P nginx dpkg --purge nginx # Configure partially installed packages dpkg --configure -a # Force install (ignore dependency errors — use with caution) dpkg --force-depends -i package.deb # Fix broken dependencies (defer to apt for this) apt install -f # recommended way to fix dpkg dependency issues

dpkg records its state in a few key files under /var/lib/dpkg/, and APT caches downloaded .deb files in /var/cache/apt/archives/. /var/lib/dpkg/status # installed package metadata /var/lib/dpkg/available # available packages from repositories /var/lib/dpkg/info/ # package scripts and file lists /var/cache/apt/archives/ # downloaded .deb package cache
APT resolves dependencies, retrieves packages from repositories, and provides a consistent interface for upgrades and searches.

Command Purpose apt update Refresh package index from repositories. apt upgrade Upgrade all installed packages (no removals). apt full-upgrade Upgrade with package removals if needed. apt install <pkg> Install a package and its dependencies. apt remove <pkg> Remove a package (keep config files). apt purge <pkg> Remove package and configuration files. apt autoremove Remove orphaned dependencies. apt autoclean Remove old cached packages. apt clean Clear all cached packages. apt search <term> Search package names and descriptions. apt show <pkg> Display detailed package information. apt list List packages (all, installed, upgradable). apt list --installed List installed packages. apt list --upgradable List packages with available updates. apt satisfies <regex> Show packages matching a dependency string. apt edit-sources Edit repository sources. apt policy <pkg> Show version and repository info.

apt-get Equivalent apt apt-get update apt update apt-get upgrade apt upgrade apt-get dist-upgrade apt full-upgrade apt-get install apt install apt-get remove apt remove apt-get purge apt purge apt-get autoremove apt autoremove apt-get autoclean apt autoclean apt-cache search apt search apt-cache show apt show apt-cache policy apt policy

These are the everyday APT operations strung together: full system updates, search–install–verify cycles, holding packages at a version, and dry-running changes before applying them. # Full system update apt update && apt upgrade -y # Search and install apt search postgres apt show postgresql apt install postgresql -y # Remove unused packages apt autoremove --purge -y # Hold a package (prevent upgrades) apt-mark hold nginx apt-mark unhold nginx apt-mark showhold # Install a specific version apt install nginx=1.24.0-1 # Reinstall a package (repair) apt install --reinstall nginx # Install without prompts DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt install -y nginx # Simulate changes (dry-run) apt install --dry-run nginx

APT pulls packages from repositories declared in /etc/apt/sources.list and the drop-in files in /etc/apt/sources.list.d/, with GPG keys verifying package authenticity. # Main sources list /etc/apt/sources.list # Additional repository files /etc/apt/sources.list.d/ # GPG keys for repository verification /etc/apt/trusted.gpg /etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d/

Each line declares one repository: the type (deb for binaries, deb-src for source code), optional [options] like architecture or signing key, the mirror URL, the distro suite, and its components. deb [options] http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu/ jammy main restricted universe multiverse deb [options] http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu/ jammy-updates main restricted deb [options] http://security.ubuntu.com/ubuntu/ jammy-security main deb-src [options] http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu/ jammy main Component Purpose main Officially supported free software. restricted Proprietary drivers (supported). universe Community-maintained free software. multiverse Non-free or restricted license software.

Third-party software ships its own repository. add-apt-repository handles the GPG key and the sources entry for you; the manual method downloads the key, writes a .list file, and refreshes the index. # Method 1: add-apt-repository (auto-adds GPG key) add-apt-repository "deb [arch=amd64] https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu jammy stable" add-apt-repository ppa:deadsnakes/ppa # Method 2: manual (add key + repo file) curl -fsSL https://example.com/gpg | gpg --dearmor -o /etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d/example.gpg echo "deb [arch=amd64 signed-by=/etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d/example.gpg] https://repo.example.com stable main" \ > /etc/apt/sources.list.d/example.list apt update
Control which repository provides each package: # /etc/apt/preferences.d/99-pin-nginx Package: nginx Pin: release a=stable Pin-Priority: 900 Package: * Pin: release a=experimental Pin-Priority: 100

nala is a drop-in replacement for apt with parallel downloads, better history, and cleaner output. # Install nala apt install nala # Basic usage (same commands as apt) nala update # parallel repository refresh nala upgrade # upgrade with progress bars nala install nginx # install with download speed display nala remove nginx nala purge nginx nala autoremove nala autopurge # autoremove + purge # History and rollback nala history # list transaction history nala history info 5 # details of transaction #5 nala history undo 5 # revert transaction #5 # Fetch (download only, don't install) nala fetch <package> # download to current directory # Show package info nala show nginx # detailed package info # Search nala search nginx # search package names/descriptions # List packages nala list --upgradable # packages with updates available nala list --installed # all installed packages

Feature APT nala Parallel downloads No Yes (16 mirrors by default) Transaction history No Yes (nala history) Rollback No Yes (nala history undo) Download progress Basic Per-package progress bars Speed Single connection Multiple mirrors simultaneously

Once a package is installed, dpkg -L lists every file it placed on disk, and dpkg -S works backwards from a path to the package that owns it. dpkg -L nginx # all files from a package dpkg -S /etc/nginx/nginx.conf # which package owns a file

Path Purpose /usr/bin/ User command binaries /usr/sbin/ System administration binaries /usr/lib/ Libraries /usr/share/ Architecture-independent data /usr/share/doc/ Package documentation /usr/share/man/ Manual pages /etc/ Configuration files /var/lib/ Variable state data /var/log/ Log files /var/cache/ Cache data

APT keeps downloaded .deb files in a local cache. Cleaning it reclaims disk space, and installing from the cache lets you work offline or reinstall without a network. # Clean package cache apt clean # remove all .deb files from /var/cache/apt/archives/ apt autoclean # remove only obsolete .deb files # Check cache size du -sh /var/cache/apt/archives/ # Install from cache (offline) dpkg -i /var/cache/apt/archives/*.deb

These commands repair common package state problems: broken dependencies, half-configured packages, corrupted files, leftover configuration, and held packages. # Fix broken dependencies apt install -f dpkg --configure -a # Reinstall a package to fix corrupt files apt install --reinstall nginx # Check for held broken packages apt-mark showhold # Verify package integrity debsums nginx # check installed files against checksums # Clean up configuration from removed packages dpkg -l | grep '^rc' # find removed-but-config-left packages dpkg --purge $(dpkg -l | grep '^rc' | awk '{print $2}') # Force reconfigure dpkg-reconfigure nginx # Find missing recommended packages apt-get check
Common Configuration Locations Linux Kernel Device Management

Every running program on a Linux system is a process. Managing processes — listing them, inspecting their resource consumption, sending signals, adjusting priorities, and controlling services — is a fundamental operations skill. This reference covers the core tools and commands for process management, from quick health checks to deep debugging.

ps takes a snapshot of running processes. The aux and -ef forms are the two most common, and -o lets you choose exactly which columns to display. ps aux # all processes, BSD-style output ps -ef # all processes, Unix-style output ps -e -o pid,ppid,user,%cpu,%mem,cmd # custom columns ps -u www-data # processes for a specific user ps -C nginx # processes matching command name ps --ppid 1234 # child processes of PID 1234 ps -eo pid,ppid,cmd --forest # process tree

Flag Column Description %cpu CPU usage Percentage of CPU time %mem Memory usage Percentage of physical memory vsz Virtual size Virtual memory in KB rss Resident size Physical memory in KB stat State Process state code start Start time When the process began time CPU time Cumulative CPU time lstart Full start Exact start timestamp nlwp Threads Number of threads

Code State Meaning R Running Executing or in run queue S Sleeping Waiting for an event (interruptible) D Uninterruptible sleep Waiting for I/O (usually disk) Z Zombie Terminated but not reaped by parent T Stopped Suspended by signal or debugger t Tracing stop Paused by ptrace < High priority Real-time or niceness < 0 N Low priority Niceness > 0

Interactive viewers refresh continuously and let you sort and act on processes with keystrokes. top ships with every system; htop, btm, and glances add color, mouse support, and more detail. top # classic interactive process viewer htop # improved color viewer (install separately) btm # bottom — modern TUI resource monitor glances # comprehensive system monitor (Python-based) top interactive keys: Key Action 1 Toggle per-CPU view M Sort by memory usage P Sort by CPU usage c Toggle full command path k Kill a process (prompts for PID and signal) r Renice a process f Select displayed columns u Filter by user q Quit

pgrep and pidof find a process's PID by name, user, or command-line pattern — handy before signaling it or inspecting its resources. pgrep nginx # list PIDs matching pattern pgrep -u www-data -f wsgi # by user and full command line pgrep -l nginx # show process name alongside PID pidof nginx # list PIDs by exact binary name
Signals tell a process to perform a specific action. The default signal for kill is TERM (15).

Number Name Action 1 SIGHUP Hangup — often used to reload configuration 2 SIGINT Interrupt from keyboard (Ctrl+C) 3 SIGQUIT Quit with core dump 9 SIGKILL Kill immediately (cannot be caught or ignored) 15 SIGTERM Terminate gracefully (default) 17 SIGCHLD Child process terminated 18 SIGCONT Continue if stopped 19 SIGSTOP Stop process (cannot be caught) kill 1234 # send SIGTERM to PID 1234 kill -9 1234 # force kill (SIGKILL) kill -HUP 1234 # reload (SIGHUP) kill -STOP 1234 # pause process kill -CONT 1234 # resume process killall nginx # kill all processes named nginx killall -HUP nginx # reload all nginx processes pkill -f "python app.py" # kill by command-line pattern pkill -u www-data # kill all processes for user kill -l # list all signal names

Nice values range from -20 (highest priority) to 19 (lowest priority). Default is 0. Only root can set negative values. nice -n 10 my_command # start with lower priority nice -n -5 my_command # start with higher priority (root) renice -n 5 -p 1234 # change priority of running process renice -n -10 -u www-data # change priority for all user processes ionice -c 2 -n 0 -p 1234 # set I/O scheduling class I/O classes: 1 = real-time, 2 = best-effort (default), 3 = idle.
systemd is the init system and service manager on modern Linux distributions. Services are defined in unit files and managed with systemctl.

systemctl controls services: start, stop, restart, reload configuration, and enable them to start automatically at boot. systemctl start nginx # start a service systemctl stop nginx # stop a service systemctl restart nginx # restart a service systemctl reload nginx # reload configuration (SIGHUP) systemctl reload-or-restart nginx # reload if supported, else restart systemctl enable nginx # enable at boot systemctl disable nginx # disable at boot systemctl enable --now nginx # enable and start systemctl mask nginx # prevent service from starting systemctl unmask nginx # allow service to start again

These commands report whether a service is running and enabled, list service units, and reveal a unit's full properties and definition. systemctl status nginx # detailed service status systemctl is-active nginx # active or inactive systemctl is-enabled nginx # enabled or disabled systemctl is-failed nginx # check if in failed state systemctl list-units --type=service # list all service units systemctl list-units --type=service --state=failed # list failed services systemctl list-unit-files --type=service # list all installed services systemctl show nginx # all service properties systemctl cat nginx # show unit file contents

journalctl filters the system journal to a specific service's output — the first stop when a service fails to start or misbehaves. journalctl -u nginx # all logs for the service journalctl -u nginx --since "1 hour ago" # recent logs journalctl -u nginx -f # follow logs journalctl -u nginx -p err # errors only

A unit file defines how and when a service runs: its description, dependencies, the process to launch, restart policy, and environment. Place it in /etc/systemd/system/ and run systemctl daemon-reload to register it. # /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service [Unit] Description=My Application After=network.target Requires=postgresql.service [Service] Type=simple User=app Group=app WorkingDirectory=/opt/myapp ExecStart=/opt/myapp/bin/server ExecReload=/bin/kill -HUP $MAINPID Restart=on-failure RestartSec=5 EnvironmentFile=/etc/myapp/env.conf StandardOutput=journal StandardError=journal [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target

Type Behavior simple Process is the main service (default); systemd assumes it starts immediately. forking Process forks and exits; parent PID expected to exit. oneshot Short-lived process; systemd waits for it to exit. notify Like simple, but sends sd_notify when ready. idle Like simple, but waits until no more jobs are active. After creating or editing a unit: systemctl daemon-reload # reload unit definitions systemctl start myapp systemctl enable myapp

These tools summarize overall memory and load. mpstat breaks CPU usage down per core, and pidstat attributes it to individual processes. free -h # memory usage summary free -h -s 5 # refresh every 5 seconds uptime # load averages (1, 5, 15 min) mpstat 1 # per-CPU statistics mpstat -P ALL 1 # all CPUs individually pidstat 1 # per-process CPU stats pidstat -u -p 1234 1 # specific PID

free and /proc/meminfo show totals; vmstat tracks memory pressure over time; pmap and smem drill into how a single process uses memory. cat /proc/meminfo # detailed memory information vmstat 1 # virtual memory statistics pmap 1234 # memory map of a process smem -k # proportional memory usage (install smem)

iostat measures disk throughput and utilization, while iotop identifies which processes are reading and writing. /proc/<pid>/fd/ and lsof show the files a process has open. iostat -x 1 # extended disk I/O stats iotop -o # top for I/O (sorted by usage) ls -l /proc/1234/fd/ # open file descriptors lsof -p 1234 # list open files for process

ss with -p links sockets to the processes that own them. nethogs and iftop show live bandwidth use by process and by connection. ss -tlnp # TCP listeners with process info ss -tunap # all TCP/UDP sockets with process nethogs eth0 # bandwidth by process (install nethogs) iftop -i eth0 # bandwidth by connection (install iftop)

The /proc virtual filesystem exposes process and kernel information. /proc/cpuinfo # CPU details /proc/meminfo # memory statistics /proc/loadavg # load averages /proc/uptime # system uptime /proc/version # kernel version /proc/sys/ # kernel tunables (sysctl) # Per-process: /proc/<pid>/cmdline # command line (null-separated) /proc/<pid>/environ # environment variables (null-separated) /proc/<pid>/fd/ # open file descriptors /proc/<pid>/status # process status and resource usage /proc/<pid>/limits # resource limits /proc/<pid>/cgroup # cgroup membership /proc/<pid>/io # I/O statistics /proc/<pid>/oom_score # OOM-killer score (0-1000, higher = more likely to kill) /proc/<pid>/oom_score_adj # OOM score adjustment (-1000 to 1000)

These ready-made command pipelines answer the common questions: what is eating CPU or memory, which process holds a port, which processes are zombie or stuck, and what a process is actually doing. # Find what's using the most CPU ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head -10 # Find what's using the most memory ps aux --sort=-%rss | head -10 # Find zombie processes (state Z: terminated but not yet reaped by parent) ps aux | awk '$8 ~ /Z/' # Find process by listening port ss -tlnp | grep ':80' # Check if a process is stuck in D state cat /proc/1234/status | grep State # Trace system calls strace -p 1234 # attach to running process strace -p 1234 -e trace=network # trace only network syscalls strace -c -p 1234 # summary counts # Trace library calls ltrace -p 1234 # Inspect child processes pstree -p 1234

SELinux (Security-Enhanced Linux) is a mandatory access control (MAC) framework built into the kernel. It originated as a set of patches from the NSA and was merged into the mainline kernel in the early 2000s. It is the default MAC implementation on RHEL, Fedora, CentOS Stream, Rocky, and AlmaLinux; Debian and Ubuntu install it only when explicitly requested, defaulting instead to AppArmor. The distinction that matters is DAC versus MAC: Discretionary access control (DAC) is the classic Unix model: owner/group/other permission bits, ACLs, and the root superuser. Access is discretionary because the object owner decides who may access it, and root can override every check. Mandatory access control (MAC) is a system-wide policy that no user, including root, may bypass. Every subject (process) and object (file, socket, port, capability) carries a label, and the kernel consults a compiled policy for every access. Even a process running as UID 0 is confined by its type. SELinux therefore does not replace DAC — it runs after DAC. A process must first pass the standard Unix permission check, then pass the SELinux check. This is why a correctly-labeled file can still be unreadable due to ordinary permissions, and why a file with 777 can still be denied by policy. What it actually protects: if an internet-facing daemon (httpd, sshd, named, postfix) is compromised, the attacker inherits that daemon's domain rather than the machine. A compromised httpd_t process cannot read /etc/shadow, rewrite sshd binaries, bind arbitrary ports, or traverse into other services' files, regardless of the UID it managed to obtain. This is confinement of the blast radius, not prevention of the initial exploit. The default targeted policy confines a defined set of system services while leaving ordinary interactive users in unconfined_t. This balances security with operational friction: most day-to-day administration is unaffected, while network-facing attack surface is confined. The stricter mls policy (multi-level security) enforces Bell-LaPadula confidentiality levels across all subjects and is uncommon outside government environments. Fedora/RHEL still run the targeted policy with MCS (multi-category security) enabled for category-based isolation. AppArmor, the default on Debian/Ubuntu, is also MAC but is path-based rather than label-based: profiles match binary paths and file paths directly rather than inode labels. This makes AppArmor easier to author but more vulnerable to path traversal and hardlink tricks; SELinux labels persist with the inode and survive renames, mounts, and hardlinks. Only one of the two is normally active on a host.

SELinux identifies every subject and object with a security context, a colon-separated string: user:role:type:level Example of a real file label (the default content label for Apache): system_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t:s0 Field Example Meaning SELinux user system_u Identity mapped from the Linux login via semanage login Role object_r RBAC role; object_r is used for all objects Type httpd_sys_content_t The type-enforcement label — the field policy actually matches on Level s0 MLS/MCS sensitivity and categories (s0:c1,c2) Type enforcement is the core mechanism. Policy rules are stated as allow <source_domain> <target_type>:<class> <permissions>, for example allow httpd_t httpd_sys_content_t:file read;. A process runs in a domain (a type applied to a process, usually ending in _t for objects and _t for domains too, e.g. httpd_t, sshd_t). Roles bind users to the domains they may enter. sysadm_r can transition to many administrative domains; user_r is limited. Role transitions are what newrole and runcon manipulate. SELinux users (user_u, staff_u, sysadm_u, unconfined_u, guest_u, xguest_u) are abstractions mapped from Unix logins. They constrain which roles a login may assume. Sensitivity and categories (the :s0:c0,c10 suffix) provide MLS/MCS compartmentalization. MCS is used in the targeted policy to isolate virtual machines and containers: two processes on the same host cannot communicate unless they share a category set. The reference policy is installed by policycoreutils and selinux-policy-targeted. The main userland tools live in policycoreutils, policycoreutils-python-utils (RHEL) or python3-setools/policycoreutils-python-utils (Debian), and setools-console provides sesearch and seinfo. # Install the tooling (RHEL/Fedora) sudo dnf install -y policycoreutils policycoreutils-python-utils selinux-policy-targeted setools-console # Install the tooling (Debian/Ubuntu) sudo apt install -y policycoreutils selinux-basics selinux-policy-default setools # Where the policy and context databases live ls /etc/selinux/targeted/contexts/files/ # file_contexts, file_contexts.local ls /etc/selinux/targeted/modules/active/ # installed modules and policy store

SELinux operates in one of three modes: enforcing (policy is applied and denials are blocked), permissive (policy violations are logged but not blocked), and disabled (no SELinux code runs and no labels are maintained). Permissive mode is the diagnostic mode; disabled is a one-way door that must be undone with a full relabel. # Quick current mode getenforce # Enforcing | Permissive | Disabled # Detailed status sestatus # mode, policy, config paths sestatus -v # verbose: contexts of key processes and files sestatus -b # current boolean values # Switch mode at runtime (until reboot) setenforce 0 # permissive setenforce 1 # enforcing The persistent configuration is /etc/selinux/config: # /etc/selinux/config SELINUX=enforcing # enforcing | permissive | disabled SELINUXTYPE=targeted # targeted | mls | minimum Changes to SELINUX and SELINUXTYPE require a reboot. SELINUXTYPE selects which policy tree under /etc/selinux/ is loaded; switching between targeted and mls requires a relabel because the expected labels differ. At boot, the kernel command line can override the config for a single boot: # Append to GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX in /etc/default/grub, then rebuild grub selinux=0 # disable SELinux entirely (no labels enforced) enforcing=0 # boot permissive regardless of config autorelabel=1 # force a full relabel at boot # Persist a kernel argument without hand-editing GRUB (RHEL/Fedora) sudo grubby --update-kernel ALL --args selinux=0 sudo grubby --update-kernel ALL --remove-args selinux Why disabling forces a relabel: when SELinux is disabled, the kernel stops maintaining the security.selinux extended attribute on new files. Files created in the meantime receive no label or an inherited stale one. Re-enabling with those unlabeled files would cause near-total denial, since policy matches on labels that are absent. The policy defaults to autorelabel=1 behavior on the first boot after re-enabling, or you trigger it manually (see Relabeling filesystems).

Most standard tools accept -Z (or --context) to append the security context column. This is the first diagnostic step for nearly every SELinux issue. # Files and directories ls -Z /var/www/html # context of each entry ls -Zd /var/www/html # context of the directory itself ll -Z ./index.html # same, with a long listing # Processes ps -Z # all processes with domain ps auxZ # full listing with domain ps -eZ | grep httpd # filter by context or command # Current user and role context id -Z # context of the shell id -Z | cut -d: -f1 # just the SELinux user # Sockets and listening ports ss -tlnpZ # TCP listeners with process and context ss -Z # all sockets with context sudo netstat -tlnpZ # legacy equivalent (deprecated) # Raw extended attribute holding the label getfattr -n security.selinux file.txt getfattr -d -m - file.txt # dump all extended attributes # Find files whose context matches a glob (SELinux-enabled findutils) find / -context '*:httpd_sys_content_t:*' 2>/dev/null # Find mislabeled or unlabeled files: restorecon -n is a dry run that # reports only the paths the current policy would relabel sudo restorecon -R -n -v /home 2>/dev/null # Inspect a context string directly secon -t # type of the current process secon -u -r -t -l file.txt # user, role, type, level of a file The -Z output is authoritative. When a denial occurs, compare the label in ls -Z against the label the policy expects, which matchpathcon prints.

Labels on disk come from a mapping between path patterns and types held in the file context database. restorecon reads that database and applies the expected label; chcon overrides it temporarily. Getting this distinction right is the crux of SELinux file administration. # chcon: change the label NOW, but not persistently (lost on relabel) chcon -t httpd_sys_content_t /var/www/html/index.html chcon -R -t httpd_sys_content_t /srv/site # recursive chcon -u system_u -r object_r -t var_t /data/db # all three label fields chcon --reference=/var/www/html /srv/site # copy label from another path chcon changes are not recorded in the policy database. A subsequent restorecon, fixfiles, or autorelabel reverts them. For anything permanent, register the mapping instead: # semanage fcontext: register a persistent path->type mapping sudo semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/srv/site(/.*)?" sudo semanage fcontext -a -e /var/www /srv/www # equivalence to an existing path sudo semanage fcontext -l # list all mappings sudo semanage fcontext -l -C # only local (custom) mappings sudo semanage fcontext -m -t httpd_sys_content_t "/srv/site(/.*)?" # modify sudo semanage fcontext -d "/srv/site(/.*)?" # delete an entry # Apply the registered mapping sudo restorecon -R -v /srv/site The regular-expression path form "/path(/.*)?" matches the directory and everything beneath it. The -a call alone does not touch the filesystem — you must run restorecon afterward to apply it. restorecon flags: restorecon -v /var/www/html/index.html # verbose: report label changes restorecon -R /srv/site # recurse restorecon -n /srv/site # dry run (show what would change) restorecon -F /srv/site # force reset even custom user labels restorecon -r /srv/site # use realpath before resolving restorecon -e /srv /srv/link # exclude a path from recursion matchpathcon prints the label policy expects for a path, making it the reference for comparison: matchpathcon /var/www/html/index.html # expected label per policy matchpathcon -V /srv/site # verify and report mismatches matchpathcon -a /srv/site # list all matching rules fixfiles drives bulk relabeling operations: sudo fixfiles relabel # relabel the whole filesystem per policy sudo fixfiles -F relabel # force, clearing user customizations sudo fixfiles restore /var/www # restore default contexts under a path sudo fixfiles -R httpd check # check files owned by an RPM package sudo fixfiles onboot # schedule a relabel for next boot sudo fixfiles -F onboot # force-relabel next boot Custom mappings are written to /etc/selinux/targeted/contexts/files/file_contexts.local. Never edit this file by hand; semanage fcontext is the supported interface. setfiles applies a context file directly and is what the boot-time relabel actually runs: sudo setfiles -v -r / /etc/selinux/targeted/contexts/files/file_contexts /srv/site

Booleans are pre-built policy switches that toggle specific allow rules on or off at runtime without recompiling policy. They let the reference policy ship permissive-by-default behavior for optional features while allowing an administrator to close it. Booleans are the correct fix when a denial is caused by policy deliberately disabling a capability, rather than by a labeling mistake. # Query getsebool httpd_can_network_connect # one boolean getsebool -a # all booleans and values semanage boolean -l # all booleans with description and defaults semanage boolean -l -C # only locally modified booleans # Set at runtime only (lost on reboot) sudo setsebool httpd_can_network_connect on sudo setsebool httpd_can_network_connect off sudo togglesebool httpd_can_network_connect # legacy flip command # Set persistently across reboots (-P required) sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on sudo setsebool -P httpd_unified off # Equivalent persistent operations via semanage sudo semanage boolean -m --on httpd_can_network_connect sudo semanage boolean -m --off httpd_read_user_content A boolean's current value is the kernel's runtime state; its persistent value is stored in the policy store. getsebool shows the former, semanage boolean -l shows both (for example (off, off) meaning current, persistent). Common booleans for services: sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on # Apache may open outbound TCP sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect_db on # Apache may reach database ports sudo setsebool -P httpd_enable_homedirs on # Apache may serve ~user/public_html sudo setsebool -P ssh_sysadm_login on # allow sysadm_r over SSH sudo setsebool -P use_nfs_home_dirs on # home directories on NFS sudo setsebool -P samba_export_all_ro on # Samba read-only export of all files sudo setsebool -P ftpd_full_access on # FTP full filesystem access sudo setsebool -P container_manage_cgroup on # containers may manage cgroups

SELinux users and roles constrain what domains a Unix login can enter. The semanage login table maps Linux accounts to SELinux users; unmapped logins fall through to the __default__ mapping. # List SELinux users and login mappings sudo semanage user -l # SELinux users, roles, MLS ranges sudo semanage login -l # Unix login -> SELinux user mapping sudo semanage login -l -C # only local custom mappings # Map a login to a SELinux user sudo semanage login -a -s staff_u jdoe # jdoe logs in as staff_u sudo semanage login -a -s user_u alice sudo semanage login -a -s sysadm_u -r s0-s0:c0.c1023 root # explicit range sudo semanage login -m -s user_u jdoe # modify an existing mapping sudo semanage login -d jdoe # delete a mapping # Change the fallback for all unmapped accounts sudo semanage login -m -s user_u __default__ The __default__ entry governs every login without an explicit mapping. On standard targeted systems it is typically unconfined_u, which is why ordinary users are unrestricted. Setting it to user_u or staff_u confines all interactive users. semanage user defines the SELinux user itself, including the roles it may assume and the MLS range: # Create a confined SELinux user with a role set sudo semanage user -a -R "staff_r system_r" -r s0 -L s0 -P user staff_u # Inspect fields: Selinux User, Roles, MLS/MCS Level, MLS/MCS Range, Prefix sudo semanage user -l # Remove a custom SELinux user sudo semanage user -d staff_u Role transitions are performed explicitly. A staff_u user entering a administrative domain runs newrole or sudo (which is policy-aware via sudo_role_transition); runcon executes a command in an arbitrary context for testing: newrole -r sysadm_r # enter a new role (prompts for password) runcon -t httpd_t -- /usr/sbin/httpd # run a single command in a context runcon system_u:system_r:httpd_t:s0 id -Z Misconfigured mappings are a common cause of "user logged in but cannot do anything": id -Z shows user_u:user_r:user_t:s0 when unconfined_u was expected.

Ports carry labels just like files. A confined daemon may only bind() a port whose type is permitted for its domain. Binding an unlisted port produces EACCES/Permission denied in the application log and an AVC in the audit log. # List port type mappings sudo semanage port -l # all port labels sudo semanage port -l -C # only local additions sudo semanage port -l | grep http # inspect an existing type # Allow a daemon to bind a non-standard port sudo semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8080 sudo semanage port -a -t ssh_port_t -p tcp 2222 sudo semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8443 sudo semanage port -m -t http_port_t -p tcp 8081 # modify existing entry sudo semanage port -d -t http_port_t -p tcp 8080 # delete a local entry # Network interface labeling sudo semanage interface -l # labeled interfaces sudo semanage interface -a -t netif_t eth1 # label an interface # Node labeling (per source address) sudo semanage node -l The well-known privileged ports (http_port_t 80, 443, 488, 8008–8009; ssh_port_t 22; smtp_port_t 25) are pre-labeled. When Apache is told to listen on 8080, the bind fails until semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8080 registers it. If the port is already claimed by another type, -a rejects it as a duplicate — use -m to reassign it instead. This is a policy guardrail: it prevents an exploited daemon from opening arbitrary ports for exfiltration or command-and-control.

When no boolean and no port/file label resolves a denial, custom policy is required. Use audit2allow -M to generate a module, but treat the generated rules as a draft to review (see Denial analysis). The reference policy is the base; modules are additive refinements loaded into the module store. # Inspect loaded modules sudo semodule -l # name and version of each module sudo semodule -l | grep myapp # Build and install sudo semodule -i myapp.pp # install a compiled module sudo semodule -r myapp # remove a module by name sudo semodule -B # rebuild policy from the module store sudo semodule -R # reload policy without recompiling sudo semodule -X 300 -i myapp.pp # install with priority 300 (higher wins) sudo semodule -X 300 -r myapp The manual workflow from CIL/.te source to a loadable module: # 1. Write the type enforcement source (myapp.te), then compile it checkmodule -M -m -o myapp.mod myapp.te # -M: enable MLS/MCS support # -m: compile to a module (not a base policy) # 2. Package the module and its file-context rules into a .pp semodule_package -o myapp.pp -m myapp.mod -f myapp.fc # 3. Install the package sudo semodule -i myapp.pp A minimal myapp.te allowing a daemon to read a custom directory resembles: policy_module(myapp, 1.0.0) type myapp_t; type myapp_exec_t; init_daemon_domain(myapp_t, myapp_exec_t) allow myapp_t var_log_t:file read; Priority (-X) matters when multiple modules define the same rules: higher-priority modules override lower-priority ones, which is how local site policy is made to win over a distribution module. semodule -i alone installs at the default priority (400 in modern policy stores; the reference distribution modules sit below it). The module store lives under /etc/selinux/targeted/modules/active/modules/; the compiled binary policy is /etc/selinux/targeted/policy/policy.NN.

Every denial is recorded by the kernel's audit subsystem. The workflow is: reproduce the failure, locate the AVC message, understand why it was denied, and only then choose a targeted fix. Audit log locations vary by distribution: # RHEL/Fedora: auditd owns the log /var/log/audit/audit.log sudo ausearch -m avc -ts recent # AVCs from the last 10 minutes sudo ausearch -m avc -ts today # Where the audit daemon is used systemctl status auditd # Ubuntu/Debian without auditd: consult the journal sudo journalctl _TRANSPORT=audit sudo journalctl -t audit | grep AVC sudo journalctl -t setroubleshoot A raw AVC record looks like: type=AVC msg=audit(1743091200.123:456): avc: denied { read } for pid=1234 comm="httpd" name="index.html" dev="sda1" ino=98765 scontext=system_u:system_r:httpd_t:s0 tcontext=unconfined_u:object_r:default_t:s0 tclass=file permissive=0 Read it as: the process in scontext (httpd_t) was denied read on the object tcontext (default_t), class file. The mismatch is almost always the target type — here default_t where httpd_sys_content_t was expected, indicating a mislabeled file. Search and summarize: sudo ausearch -m avc -ts recent # recent AVCs sudo ausearch -m avc -ts 09/24/2026 00:00:00 # since a timestamp sudo ausearch -m avc -c httpd # filter by command sudo ausearch -m avc -p 1234 # filter by PID sudo ausearch -m avc -su unconfined_u # filter by source user sudo aureport -a # summary report of AVCs by type # Trace a reported issue through the full record sudo ausearch -m avc -i | tail -50 Interpretation tools. audit2why explains the policy reason for a denial (missing allow, boolean off, constraint); audit2allow drafts allow rules from logged denials: sudo ausearch -m avc -ts recent | audit2why # human-readable reason sudo ausearch -m avc -ts recent | audit2allow # proposed allow rules sudo ausearch -m avc -c httpd -ts today | audit2allow # only httpd denials sudo audit2allow -a # scan the whole audit log sudo audit2allow -a -M mypolicy # generate mypolicy.te/.pp sudo semodule -i mypolicy.pp # install after review sudo audit2allow -i /var/log/audit/audit.log -w # list why-denied explanations Warning — do not blanket-allow. audit2allow writes the most permissive rule that silences each denial, including rules that would defeat the confinement you rely on. A generated allow httpd_t shadow_t:file read; is a legitimate cryptographic-module access or an exfiltration path depending on context, and audit2allow cannot tell them apart. Always read every generated rule, prefer a boolean or a relabel when one fits, and never paste audit2allow output blindly into production. The tool answers "how do I make the denial stop", not "what is the correct policy". setroubleshoot/sealert pre-translate AVCs into human explanations and suggested fixes: sudo dnf install -y setroubleshoot-server # RHEL/Fedora package systemctl status setroubleshootd sudo sealert -a /var/log/audit/audit.log # analyze all AVCs sudo sealert -l 3ff... # detail a specific alert by ID sudo sealert -b # open the GUI alert browser # setools query the policy directly sesearch -A -s httpd_t -t httpd_sys_content_t # all allows for a pair sesearch -A -s httpd_t -t http_port_t -c tcp_socket # all allow rules seinfo -t | grep httpd # types matching a name seinfo -x -t httpd_t # aliases

A relabel rewrites every security.selinux extended attribute on the filesystem to the label the current policy expects. It is required after re-enabling SELinux, after restoring a backup that did not preserve extended attributes, and after significant policy changes. Relabeling is safe for labels but can take a long time on large or slow filesystems; the machine is best left to complete it. # Schedule a full relabel for the next boot sudo touch /.autorelabel sudo reboot # Same, via fixfiles (also supports forced relabel) sudo fixfiles onboot sudo fixfiles -F onboot # Relabel now, without rebooting sudo fixfiles relabel # Target only one tree sudo restorecon -R -v /srv/site sudo fixfiles restore /var/www # Force reset of user-customized labels during a relabel sudo fixfiles -F relabel The boot-time mechanism matters: the GUI/CLI relabel can be interrupted, leaving labels half-applied, whereas /.autorelabel performs a clean relabel during early boot before services start, then reboots again on completion. Expect two reboots and a delay proportional to file count; fixfiles prints progress and reports the number of files examined. genhomedircon regenerates the per-user home-directory context rules when SELinux users are added or changed: sudo genhomedircon # regenerate /etc/selinux/targeted/contexts/files/homedir_template output sudo semodule -B # regeneration is also triggered by a policy rebuild On systems with truly enormous filesystems, relabeling every inode can take hours. It is more practical to relabel per-tree with restorecon -R for the paths that matter than to force a full pass.

Container runtimes and SELinux interact at the volume-mount boundary. The default container_t domain (historically svirt_lxc_net_t for the sandbox) cannot access host files labeled for general use, so a bind-mounted volume must be relabeled for the container to read it. # Bind-mount with a label podman run -v /host/data:/data:z nginx # :z — shared label (multiple containers) podman run -v /host/data:/data:Z nginx # :Z — private label (this container only) docker run -v /host/data:/data:z nginx # Docker with SELinux support enabled :z relabels the host path for shared access: multiple containers may mount it. :Z relabels the host path exclusively for one container; conflicting containers are denied. It is private and mutually exclusive with :z. Both are destructive to host labels — the source directory's label is changed on the host, and any process outside the container group requiring the original label (for example, a host httpd) will then be denied. Manual equivalent when not using a runtime label flag: # Older/MLS sandbox type sudo chcon -Rt svirt_sandbox_file_t /host/data # Modern container type sudo chcon -Rt container_file_t /host/data sudo restorecon -R -v /host/data # revert once the container is done # Persistent type for a host directory intended for containers sudo semanage fcontext -a -t container_file_t "/srv/containers(/.*)?" sudo restorecon -R /srv/containers # Containers that run systemd or manage cgroups need a boolean sudo setsebool -P container_manage_cgroup on # Generate a confinement policy for a container sudo dnf install -y udica sudo udica -j /path/to/container.json mycontainer # produce mycontainer.cil Docker generally requires SELinux support to be enabled in the daemon and may need --security-opt label=disable for images that fight confinement; doing so removes the isolation and should be a deliberate choice. Podman integrates SELinux natively, including per-container MCS categories, and is the recommended runtime on RHEL-family hosts. Rootless Podman relabels user data in the user's namespace and does not affect host labels outside the container's user.

# 1. Allow a web server on a non-standard port (8080) sudo semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8080 sudo firewall-cmd --add-port=8080/tcp --permanent # open the firewall too sudo firewall-cmd --reload sudo systemctl restart httpd # 2. Serve content from a custom directory sudo semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/srv/site(/.*)?" sudo restorecon -R -v /srv/site sudo systemctl restart httpd # Alternatively, tag the tree httpd_sys_rw_content_t if the app must write. # 3. Fix a mislabeled home directory (e.g. after a restore or rsync) sudo restorecon -R -v /home/jdoe sudo restorecon -R -v /home/jdoe/.ssh sudo semanage fcontext -a -e /home /export/home # if homes are elsewhere # 4. Diagnose an SSH or nginx denial end to end sudo ausearch -m avc -ts recent sudo ausearch -m avc -c nginx -ts today | audit2why sudo restorecon -R -v /var/www /etc/nginx # relabel the serving tree sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on # if nginx proxies upstream # 5. Allow a service to make outbound network connections sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect_db on # 6. Allow Samba to share a non-default path sudo semanage fcontext -a -t samba_share_t "/srv/samba/share(/.*)?" sudo restorecon -R -v /srv/samba/share # 7. Bind a service to a privileged custom port sudo semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8443 # 8. Revert an ad-hoc chcon after confirming the permanent mapping sudo restorecon -R -v /srv/site

Disabling SELinux removes confinement for every process on the host and is a last resort, not a tuning step. A targeted setsebool, a semanage fcontext, or a small policy module is almost always the correct fix; disabling trades away the entire security property the system was built with. On RHEL-family systems, note that the vendor support statement expects SELinux to be enabled, and some compliance regimes (PCI-DSS, STIG, CIS Level 2) require it. If it must be disabled, do it cleanly so that re-enabling later is not catastrophic: # 1. Take the system permissive first (verify the app works without confinement) sudo setenforce 0 # 2. Make the change persistent sudo sed -i 's/^SELINUX=.*/SELINUX=disabled/' /etc/selinux/config grep '^SELINUX' /etc/selinux/config # 3. Disable at the kernel level as well (takes effect after reboot) sudo grubby --update-kernel ALL --args selinux=0 # 4. Reboot to apply sudo reboot Re-enabling requires a full relabel, because files created while SELinux was disabled carry missing or stale labels: sudo sed -i 's/^SELINUX=.*/SELINUX=enforcing/' /etc/selinux/config sudo grubby --update-kernel ALL --remove-args selinux sudo touch /.autorelabel sudo reboot # relabels on boot, then reboots once more Caveats: disabling is not isolated to the machine if it is joined to a domain or managed by configuration management that asserts SELinux state; it will be re-enabled by the next provisioning run. Permissive mode should be used for diagnosis (it logs the denials that enforcing would block) and never left on permanently, because it gives the false impression that SELinux is providing protection while allowing every access. On Debian/Ubuntu, if SELinux was never enabled, the correct move is usually to remove the packages rather than half-configure a disabled stack.

Sound and video on Linux are handled by two largely independent stacks. Audio flows from the kernel's ALSA layer up to a userspace sound server — typically PipeWire (modern) or PulseAudio (legacy) — while video output is handled by the kernel DRM/KMS layer and configured per display server (X11 or Wayland). Input devices such as microphones and webcams sit on top of ALSA and V4L2 respectively. This reference covers detecting the hardware, inspecting and switching device profiles, configuring the stacks, and debugging them.

Start by identifying what the kernel sees. Audio controllers and GPUs appear on the PCI bus; USB microphones, webcams, and Bluetooth adapters appear on the USB bus. # Audio and graphics controllers on PCI lspci | grep -i audio # sound cards / controllers lspci | grep -iE 'vga|3d|display' # GPUs / display controllers lspci -k # show the kernel driver bound to each device # USB peripherals (mics, webcams, Bluetooth adapters) lsusb # list USB devices lsusb -t # USB hierarchy tree # Audio devices known to ALSA aplay -l # playback devices (speakers) arecord -l # capture devices (microphones) # Video capture devices (webcams, capture cards) v4l2-ctl --list-devices # V4L2 devices (install v4l-utils) /proc/asound/ exposes ALSA's view of the cards, and /sys/class/drm/ lists display connectors. cat /proc/asound/cards # ALSA sound cards cat /proc/asound/devices # ALSA PCM devices ls /sys/class/drm/ # DRM connectors (card0-HDMI-A-1, etc.)

Layer Component Role Kernel ALSA Drivers and hardware access Session PipeWire + WirePlumber Modern sound server and policy manager Legacy PulseAudio Older sound server, still common Legacy JACK Low-latency pro-audio (often bridged by PipeWire) PipeWire exposes PulseAudio, JACK, and ALSA compatibility interfaces, so most applications and commands from other stacks still work against it.

ALSA is the kernel-level interface. Its CLI tools talk directly to hardware, bypassing the sound server — useful for testing whether a device works at all. aplay -l # list playback devices arecord -l # list capture devices aplay -L # list all PCM definitions (incl. plugins) # Play / record aplay -D plughw:0,0 file.wav # play through card 0, device 0 aplay -D default file.wav # play through the default device arecord -f cd -d 5 test.wav # record 5s CD-quality audio speaker-test -c 2 -t wav # test left/right channels # Mixer control amixer # list controls for the default card amixer -c 0 sset Master 80% # set Master volume to 80% amixer -c 0 sset Master mute # mute alsamixer # interactive ncurses mixer (F6 selects card)

ALSA settings are defined in asound.conf (system-wide) and ~/.asoundrc (per-user). /etc/asound.conf # system-wide ALSA config ~/.asoundrc # per-user ALSA config # Example: make card 1, device 0 the default output # ~/.asoundrc # default.pcm.card 1 # default.pcm.device 0 # default.ctl.card 1

PipeWire is the modern sound server; WirePlumber is its session/policy manager and decides which device becomes the default. Both run as user services. # Service status and control systemctl --user status pipewire # sound server systemctl --user status wireplumber # session manager systemctl --user restart pipewire pipewire-pulse wireplumber

wpctl is the everyday tool for inspecting and changing devices, volumes, and defaults. wpctl status # devices, sinks, sources, streams wpctl status -n # hide unavailable nodes wpctl set-volume @DEFAULT_AUDIO_SINK@ 0.5 # set sink volume (0.0–1.0) wpctl set-volume -l 1.5 @DEFAULT_AUDIO_SINK@ 0.1 # limit max to 150% wpctl set-mute @DEFAULT_AUDIO_SINK@ toggle # toggle mute wpctl set-default <ID> # set default sink/source by ID wpctl inspect <ID> # full properties of a node wpctl status # IDs are listed in brackets

pw-cli info all # dump all PipeWire objects pw-cli ls Node # list nodes pw-dump # JSON dump of the graph (inspect/machine-readable) pw-top # live CPU and xrun/quantum stats pw-link -l # list links between ports pw-metadata -n settings # inspect global settings

Configuration lives system-wide under /etc/pipewire/ and per-user under ~/.config/pipewire/, with WirePlumber equivalents. User files override system files of the same name. /etc/pipewire/ # system config ~/.config/pipewire/ # user overrides /etc/wireplumber/ # system WirePlumber policy ~/.config/wireplumber/ # user WirePlumber policy # Drop-in overrides (preferred, avoids replacing upstream files) ~/.config/pipewire/pipewire.conf.d/ # main daemon settings ~/.config/wireplumber/wireplumber.conf.d/ # routing/default policy

If PipeWire's PulseAudio compatibility layer is active, the pactl/pacmd commands below still work and target PipeWire. On a pure PulseAudio system they target the daemon directly. pactl info # server info (name, version, defaults) pactl list short sinks # outputs pactl list short sources # inputs pactl list short modules # loaded modules pactl list cards # cards and their available profiles pactl set-default-sink <name> # switch default output pactl set-default-source <name> # switch default input pactl set-sink-volume <name> 50% # set volume pactl set-sink-mute <name> toggle # toggle mute pactl set-card-profile <card> <profile> # switch a card profile pactl load-module module-loopback latency_msec=1 # example module load pactl unload-module <index> # unload a module pacmd list-sinks # verbose alternative Configuration files: /etc/pulse/default.pa # system defaults /etc/pulse/client.conf # client settings ~/.config/pulse/ # per-user config and runtime state ~/.config/pulse/default.pa # user overrides (copy from /etc/pulse)

A sound card (especially one with both analog and digital I/O, or a Bluetooth headset) exposes multiple profiles — combinations of inputs and outputs. Choosing the right profile is the usual fix for "no sound" or "microphone missing" problems. # List a card's profiles pactl list cards | grep -A 30 -i 'Profiles' pactl list cards | grep -iE 'Active Profile|Name:' # Switch profile (example: A2DP vs. headset/HFP) pactl set-card-profile bluez_card.XX_XX_XX_XX_XX_XX a2dp-sink pactl set-card-profile bluez_card.XX_XX_XX_XX_XX_XX headset-head-unit # With PipeWire/WirePlumber, list profile-capable nodes and switch by ID wpctl status wpctl inspect <ID> Common profile suffixes: Suffix Meaning analog-stereo Analog output + input digital-stereo / iec958 S/PDIF or HDMI digital passthrough hdmi-stereo HDMI audio output a2dp-sink Bluetooth high-quality audio (output only) headset-head-unit / hfp Bluetooth duplex with microphone (lower quality) off Card disabled

Bluetooth audio is handled by BlueZ (the daemon) plus WirePlumber/PulseAudio for the audio profiles. The adapter must be powered on and the device paired and trusted. systemctl status bluetooth # BlueZ daemon rfkill list # check for a soft/hard block rfkill unblock bluetooth # clear a soft block if blocked bluetoothctl # interactive shell # Inside bluetoothctl: # power on # agent on # default-agent # scan on # devices # list discovered devices # pair XX:XX:XX:XX:XX:XX # trust XX:XX:XX:XX:XX:XX # auto-reconnect on future sessions # connect XX:XX:XX:XX:XX:XX # info XX:XX:XX:XX:XX:XX # show connection and profile state # scan off # quit # Non-interactive bluetoothctl power on bluetoothctl scan on bluetoothctl pair XX:XX:XX:XX:XX:XX bluetoothctl trust XX:XX:XX:XX:XX:XX bluetoothctl connect XX:XX:XX:XX:XX:XX bluetoothctl info XX:XX:XX:XX:XX:XX bluetoothctl disconnect XX:XX:XX:XX:XX:XX bluetoothctl remove XX:XX:XX:XX:XX:XX # Inspect the adapter and pairing state hciconfig -a # adapter details (legacy bluez-tools) bluetoothctl show # adapter status and settings

High-quality audio uses A2DP with a codec negotiated between the source and the headset. WirePlumber exposes codec selection via node properties. # List the codec a connected device is using (WirePlumber) wpctl inspect <ID> | grep -i codec # PipeWire Bluetooth config override # /etc/pipewire/pipewire.conf.d/bluez.conf # wireplumber.settings = { # bluetooth.autoswitch-to-headset-profile = false # } # WirePlumber codec/feature policy # ~/.config/wireplumber/wireplumber.conf.d/bluetooth.conf Common A2DP codecs: SBC (always available), AAC, aptX/aptX HD, LDAC. Availability depends on the adapter, the headset, and installed codec plugins.
Video output runs through kernel DRM/KMS; the userspace configuration tool depends on the display server.

xrandr # list outputs, modes, and current state xrandr --query # same as above # Enable and position displays xrandr --output HDMI-1 --auto --right-of eDP-1 xrandr --output DP-1 --mode 2560x1440 --rate 144 xrandr --output HDMI-1 --off # disable a display # Mirror displays xrandr --output HDMI-1 --same-as eDP-1 # Scaling (fractional) xrandr --output eDP-1 --scale 1.25x1.25 # Rotate xrandr --output eDP-1 --rotate left # Set a display as primary xrandr --output eDP-1 --primary arandr provides a graphical front-end that emits the equivalent xrandr command.

Wayland compositors have their own display tools — there is no universal xrandr equivalent. # wlroots-based compositors (Sway, Hyprland, etc.) wlr-randr # list outputs wlr-randr --output HDMI-A-1 --mode 1920x1080 --scale 1.5 # GNOME gnome-randr # community tool; GNOME 47+ has built-in display config # KDE Plasma kscreen-doctor -o # list outputs kscreen-doctor output.HDMI-A-1.mode.1920x1080@60

ls /sys/class/drm/ # connectors and their status cat /sys/class/drm/card0-HDMI-A-1/status # "connected" or "disconnected" cat /sys/class/drm/card0-HDMI-A-1/modes # modes the display advertises drm_info # DRM device details (install drm-info) modetest -M <driver> # low-level KMS test tool (libdrm-tests)

nvidia-smi # NVIDIA GPU status and processes nvidia-settings # NVIDIA X config (when installed) glxinfo | grep -i "OpenGL renderer" # active GL renderer vainfo # hardware video acceleration support (VA-API)

arecord -l # capture devices arecord -f cd -d 5 mic-test.wav # record a test clip aplay mic-test.wav # play it back aplay -D hw:1,0 mic-test.wav # bypass the sound server amixer -c 1 sset Capture 80% # set capture gain amixer -c 1 sset Capture cap # enable capture alsamixer # capture controls are under F4 # Through the sound server wpctl status # find the source ID wpctl set-volume <ID> 0.8 # set source volume wpctl set-mute <ID> toggle # mute/unmute a source pactl list short sources # list sources (PulseAudio-compatible)

Video capture uses the kernel V4L2 interface. v4l2-ctl --list-devices # list capture devices and /dev/video* nodes v4l2-ctl -d /dev/video0 --list-formats-ext # supported resolutions and formats v4l2-ctl -d /dev/video0 --list-ctrls # controls (brightness, exposure, etc.) v4l2-ctl -d /dev/video0 --set-fmt-video=width=1920,height=1080 # Quick capture test ffmpeg -f v4l2 -i /dev/video0 -frames:v 1 snapshot.jpg ffplay /dev/video0 # preview the camera # Camera control GUI guvcview # or: cheese

dmesg | grep -iE 'snd|audio|pipewire' # audio-related kernel messages dmesg | grep -iE 'drm|hdmi|nvidia' # display-related kernel messages dmesg | grep -iE 'usb|bluetooth' # USB/Bluetooth enumeration journalctl --user -u pipewire -b # PipeWire logs this boot journalctl --user -u wireplumber -b # WirePlumber logs this boot journalctl -u bluetooth -b # BlueZ logs this boot

No sound: check the active profile (pactl list cards), the default sink (wpctl status / pactl info), and mute state. Restart the user services: systemctl --user restart pipewire pipewire-pulse wireplumber Bluetooth device won't reconnect: bluetoothctl trust the device, then connect. Toggle the adapter with bluetoothctl power off && bluetoothctl power on. Bluetooth mic unusable: the headset must switch from a2dp-sink to headset-head-unit; this lowers output quality but enables the mic. Monitor not detected: confirm the connector shows connected in /sys/class/drm/, then re-scan displays (xrandr or wlr-randr) or check dmesg for link training errors. Webcam busy: another process holds /dev/video*; find it with fuser -v /dev/video0 or lsof /dev/video0.
systemctl --user stop pipewire pipewire-pulse wireplumber rm -rf ~/.local/state/wireplumber/* # reset WirePlumber policy state systemctl --user start pipewire pipewire-pulse wireplumber

Purpose Path ALSA (system / user) /etc/asound.conf, ~/.asoundrc PipeWire (system / user) /etc/pipewire/, ~/.config/pipewire/ WirePlumber (system / user) /etc/wireplumber/, ~/.config/wireplumber/ PulseAudio (system / user) /etc/pulse/, ~/.config/pulse/ Bluetooth (BlueZ) /etc/bluetooth/main.conf X11 display config /etc/X11/xorg.conf.d/, ~/.xprofile DRM/KMS (kernel) /sys/class/drm/

SSH (Secure Shell) is the standard protocol for securely connecting to and managing remote Linux systems. Beyond interactive shells, SSH provides encrypted file transfer, port forwarding, agent forwarding, and key-based authentication — all essential for daily operations work.

An SSH key pair consists of a private key kept on your machine and a public key installed on servers. ssh-keygen creates and manages both; Ed25519 is the recommended algorithm for new keys. # Generate an Ed25519 key (modern, recommended) ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "john@example.com" # Generate an RSA key (4096-bit) ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -C "john@example.com" # Generate with specific filename ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/prod_key -C "production access" # Change passphrase on existing key ssh-keygen -p -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 # Inspect a public key ssh-keygen -l -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

Type Algorithm Recommendation ed25519 Ed25519 Preferred — fast, compact, secure rsa (3072+) RSA Fallback for older servers ecdsa ECDSA P-256 curve; usable but Ed25519 is better dsa DSA Deprecated — avoid

ssh-copy-id installs your public key into the remote account's authorized_keys, enabling password-less logins. ssh-copy-id user@remote-host # copy default key ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/prod_key user@host # copy specific key ssh-copy-id -p 2222 user@host # non-standard port Manual method if ssh-copy-id is unavailable: cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub | ssh user@host "mkdir -p ~/.ssh && cat >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys"

The basic ssh invocation opens an interactive shell on a remote host. Common options select a non-standard port, a specific identity file, and the verbosity level for diagnosing connection problems. ssh user@host # standard connection ssh -p 2222 user@host # non-standard port ssh -i ~/.ssh/prod_key user@host # specific identity file ssh -v user@host # verbose (debugging connection issues) ssh -vvv user@host # very verbose

Beyond interactive shells, SSH can run a single remote command, pipe a local script to a remote shell, or hop through a jump host to reach hosts in a private network. # Run a single command ssh user@host "uptime" ssh user@host "sudo systemctl restart nginx" # Run a local script on a remote host ssh user@host "bash -s" < local_script.sh # Multi-hop (jump host) ssh -J jump-user@bastion.internal target-user@10.0.1.50 # Escape sequences (from an active session) ~. # force disconnect ~^Z # background the connection ~? # list escape sequences
The ~/.ssh/config file allows persistent per-host connection settings.

Persistent settings for a host live in a config block: an alias, the real hostname, user, port, and identity file. Wildcard patterns apply shared defaults to groups of hosts. # ~/.ssh/config Host prod-web-1 HostName 10.0.1.50 User deploy Port 22 IdentityFile ~/.ssh/prod_key Host prod-web-2 HostName 10.0.1.51 User deploy IdentityFile ~/.ssh/prod_key # Wildcard patterns Host staging-* User ubuntu IdentityFile ~/.ssh/staging_key StrictHostKeyChecking no UserKnownHostsFile /dev/null Host *.internal ProxyJump bastion.internal User admin

Option Purpose Example HostName Target hostname or IP HostName 10.0.0.5 User Username User deploy Port SSH port Port 2222 IdentityFile Private key path IdentityFile ~/.ssh/prod_key ProxyJump Jump host ProxyJump bastion ForwardAgent Agent forwarding ForwardAgent yes ServerAliveInterval Keep-alive interval ServerAliveInterval 60 ServerAliveCountMax Max keep-alive count ServerAliveCountMax 5 Compression Enable compression Compression yes StrictHostKeyChecking Accept unknown hosts StrictHostKeyChecking accept-new UserKnownHostsFile Known hosts file UserKnownHostsFile ~/.ssh/known_hosts LocalForward Local port forward LocalForward 5432 db.internal:5432 RemoteForward Remote port forward RemoteForward 8080 localhost:80

Keep-alive settings prevent idle connections from being dropped by NATs or firewalls. Configure them per-connection on the client side, or globally for all sessions on the server. # Client-side keep-alive ssh -o ServerAliveInterval=60 -o ServerAliveCountMax=5 user@host # Server-side keep-alive (/etc/ssh/sshd_config) ClientAliveInterval 60 ClientAliveCountMax 5

Access a remote service through an SSH tunnel: # Forward local port 8080 to remote:80 ssh -L 8080:localhost:80 user@web-server # Forward local port 5432 to a database via a jump host ssh -L 5432:db.internal:5432 user@bastion # Access remote service on localhost:8080 curl http://localhost:8080

Expose a local service to a remote host: # Expose local port 3000 to remote:8080 ssh -R 8080:localhost:3000 user@public-server # Now others on public-server can access your local service via port 8080
Create a SOCKS proxy through the SSH connection: ssh -D 1080 user@bastion # Configure browser to use SOCKS5 proxy at localhost:1080

Adding -fN sends the connection to the background after authentication and suppresses the remote shell — useful for keeping a tunnel open without occupying a terminal. ssh -fN -L 5432:db.internal:5432 user@bastion # -f: background, -N: no remote command
The ssh-agent holds decrypted private keys in memory, so you only type your passphrase once per session.

The agent keeps decrypted keys in memory so you only enter your passphrase once per session. Start it, add your keys, then list what is loaded to confirm. eval "$(ssh-agent)" # start a new agent ssh-add # add default key (~/.ssh/id_rsa, etc.) ssh-add ~/.ssh/prod_key # add a specific key ssh-add -l # list loaded keys ssh-add -L # list public keys ssh-add -d ~/.ssh/prod_key # remove a key ssh-add -D # remove all keys ssh-add -t 3600 ~/.ssh/prod_key # add key with 1-hour lifetime

Agent forwarding lets you use your local keys on a remote host without copying them: ssh -A user@bastion # forward agent ssh -A -J user@bastion 10.0.1.50 # jump host with agent forwarding Security note: Agent forwarding exposes your agent socket to the remote host. Use with caution on untrusted servers, or prefer ProxyJump (which doesn't expose the agent).

These hardened sshd_config settings enforce key-only authentication: disable root login and password auth, restrict which users may log in, and set timeouts to kill idle sessions. Port 22 PermitRootLogin no PasswordAuthentication no PubkeyAuthentication yes AuthorizedKeysFile .ssh/authorized_keys AllowUsers deploy admin MaxAuthTries 3 ClientAliveInterval 60 ClientAliveCountMax 5 X11Forwarding no After editing: sshd -t # test configuration syntax systemctl reload sshd # apply changes without dropping connections systemctl restart sshd # restart sshd (may drop existing sessions)

The authorized_keys file grants login access to the matching private key. Each line holds one public key, and options at the start of a line can restrict what that key may do. # ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (one key per line) ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3... deploy@host # Restrict a key to a single command command="/opt/backup/run.sh" ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3... backup-bot # Restrict a key by source IP from="10.0.0.0/8" ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3... internal-user

scp copies files securely over SSH — to and from remote hosts, recursively for directories, and with attribute preservation. # Copy to remote scp file.txt user@host:/path/to/destination/ scp -P 2222 file.txt user@host:~/app/ # Copy from remote scp user@host:/var/log/syslog ./logs/ # Recursive copy scp -r configs/ user@host:/etc/myapp/ # Preserve attributes scp -p file.txt user@host:/tmp/

rsync efficiently synchronizes files between local and remote systems with delta transfers. # Basic sync to remote rsync -avz ./www/ user@host:/var/www/ # Sync from remote rsync -avz user@host:/var/log/ ./logs/ # Dry-run (preview without transferring) rsync -avzn ./www/ user@host:/var/www/ # Delete files on destination that don't exist on source rsync -avz --delete ./www/ user@host:/var/www/ # Common flags rsync -avP ./dir/ user@host:/dir/ # archive mode, verbose, show progress Flag Effect -a Archive mode: recursive, preserve permissions, timestamps, symlinks -v Verbose -z Compress during transfer -P Show progress and keep partial files -n Dry-run --delete Remove files on dest not present on source --exclude Exclude patterns (e.g., --exclude='*.log') -e "ssh -p 2222" Use specific SSH port

sftp provides an interactive, FTP-style session over SSH for browsing, uploading, and downloading files. sftp user@host # interactive FTP-like session sftp -P 2222 user@host # non-standard port Interactive commands: ls, cd, get, put, mget, mput, rm, mkdir, bye.

Work through connection failures systematically: increase verbosity, check DNS and port reachability, verify known_hosts and key permissions, and inspect the server's authentication logs. # Verbose connection attempts ssh -vvv user@host # Check DNS dig +short host.example.com # Check port reachability nc -zv host.example.com 22 telnet host.example.com 22 # Check known_hosts issues ssh-keygen -R host.example.com # remove host from known_hosts ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no user@host # skip host key check (insecure) # Check key permissions ls -la ~/.ssh/ # Should be: dir=700, private keys=600, public keys=644 chmod 700 ~/.ssh chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_* chmod 644 ~/.ssh/id_*.pub # Check server logs ssh user@host "sudo tail -50 /var/log/auth.log" # Debian ssh user@host "sudo tail -50 /var/log/secure" # RHEL
